confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: [p. 30] Stress is not phonemic. In so far as the initial syllable of polysyllabic words has frequently more than weakest stress, stress has a certain delimiting function. But it is largely determined by the relative sonority or weight of the syllables and/or by rhythmic factors, such as the number and character of the syllables within the words as well as in phrases. In phrases and sentences the rhythmic factors may be decisive but they are difficult to determine. ... The most important factor of sonority is the vowel length. In disyllabic word forms with a short final syllable the initial syllable, short or long, has the stronger stress in all the dialects ... In forms with a long vowel in the second syllable the stronger stress shifts to the final syllable, while a preceding syllable with a short vowel has a stronger stress in Atkan (1952) than in Eastern ... With long vowels in both syllables the stress is rather even ... [p. 31] In Eastern the stronger stress tends to fall on the next to the last syllable if the last one is short, but it may also be attracted by a sonorous consonant to the preceding syllable ... In Atkan the stronger stress tends to fall on the initial syllable of a trisyllabic form but it may also be attracted by a sonorous consonant to the following syllable ... Forms with four short syllables tend to have a trochaic rhythm but relatively sonorous consonants may break it ... Long vowels attract stress also in longer forms
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Aleut is not in the catalog. All six title-keyword items (Taff 1992, Bergsland 1983, Rozelle 1997, Asinovsky & Golovko 1987, Oshima 1990, Oshima 1994; the Miyaoka & Endo 1994 record is a duplicate of Oshima 1994) turned out to be scanned online at the Alaska Native Language Archive (https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/<id>/<id>; old uaf.edu URLs are dead, the record API ishttps://uafanlc.alaska.edu/drupal/api/record?identifier=<id> with an incomplete TLS chain) — all downloaded, scanned (tesseract, 300 dpi, sequential) and read; plus Bergsland's 1997 reference grammar (ERIC microfiche text on archive.org) read at sec. 1.2.2.1. Everything is under with. Consistent picture: stress is non-phonemic and quantity/sonority-driven; Eastern Aleut = penultimate (mora) with a heavy final syllable attracting stress unless the penult is also heavy (Taff 1992 rule; Rozelle 1997 acoustic confirmation, stress assigned before final-syllable deletion; Oshima 1990/1994 'primary stress on the penultimate mora, secondary on the initial mora'); Atkan/Attuan = fluctuating with initial tendency (Bergsland 1983, 1997), and Asinovsky & Golovko 1987 claim Bering Island Aleut has no word stress, only an alternating rhythmic accent reset at long vowels. Only unread relevant item: Taff et al. 2001 J. Phonetics 29 (paywalled DOI 10.1006/jpho.2001.0142), medium priority.org, Crossref and the grammar's bibliography.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and partly fluctuating. Long vowels attract the strongest stress (a long final vowel takes it in disyllables; long vowels attract it in longer forms too). Among short syllables the default differs by dialect: Eastern Aleut (Unalaska, Pribilof, Umnak) tends to penultimate stress when the final syllable is short (last syllable if long); Atkan/Attuan tends to initial stress. Sonorous consonants, closed syllables and phrase rhythm can pull stress one syllable away from the default. Bergsland 1994 (Dictionary p. xx) gives the same rule more compactly: Eastern stronger stress on the penult if the last syllable is short, on the last if it is long, weaker stress frequently on the first syllable; Atkan/Attuan initial stress more prevalent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: The initial syllable of polysyllables 'has frequently more than weakest stress' (delimiting function); 1994: 'a weaker stress frequently falls on the first syllable'; four short syllables tend to a trochaic rhythm. Oshima 1990/1994 (Umnak Eastern): secondary stress on the initial mora, primary on the penultimate mora, alternating backwards; Taff 1992 (Pribilof): iterative rhythmic secondary stresses, moraic feet built right-to-left.
new_statements.exceptions: Sonorous consonants (y, l, nasals) attract stress to a neighbouring syllable (tayagux vs tagayux 'salt'); the same word is stressed differently in different contexts by phrase rhythm (ataqan tayagux stressed two ways in one 1952 text); with long vowels in both syllables stress is 'rather even'; emphatic stress on the initial syllable with gemination (sec. 1.6.1); exclamatory final stress with lengthening and raised pitch (1.6.2); Eastern syncopation interacts with stress. Asinovsky & Golovko 1987 and Golovko 1997 describe Bering Island Aleut as having no word stress, only an alternating rhythmic accent reset by long vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Word forms observed in recorded texts and phrases (Atkan 1952 tapes, Eastern 1909 cylinders, 1982-84 fieldwork); Bergsland notes rhythmic factors in phrases can be decisive and hard to weigh, so citation forms and connected speech may differ. Covers all dialects with an Eastern vs Atkan/Attuan split.
new_statements.identity_note: Bergsland 1997 covers the whole language (Eastern = Unalaska/Pribilof/Umnak; Western = Atkan and Attuan; Commander Islands) and states an Eastern-vs-Atkan difference in default stress. Taff 1992 and Rozelle 1997 describe Pribilof (Eastern) Aleut; Oshima 1990/1994 describe Umnak (Eastern); Asinovsky & Golovko 1987 and Golovko 1997 describe Bering Island (Commander) Aleut, a conservative Atkan variety, and deny word stress there.

new_statements.citation: Bergsland, Knut. 1997. Aleut Grammar: Unangam Tunuganaan Achixaasix (ANLC Research Paper 10). Fairbanks: Alaska Native Language Center.
new_statements.reading: Aleut word stress is non-phonemic and weight-driven (long vowel = heavy), with a dialect split at the right edge: Eastern (Umnak/Pribilof/Akutan) is penultimate by default, with a heavy (long-vowel) final syllable taking the stress unless the penult is also heavy (Taff 1992; Rozelle 1997 confirms acoustically; Oshima 1990/1994 state it as 'penultimate mora'), plus sonorant-consonant attraction and free variation; Atkan/Attuan (incl. Bering Island) is initial-leaning and fluctuating, and Asinovsky & Golovko 1987 deny word stress for Bering Island Aleut altogether in favour of an alternating rhythmic accent reset by long vowels. For a language-level coding: quantity-sensitive right-edge (penult, final if heavy) for Eastern; variable/initial for Atkan. Bergsland 1997 is the reference grammar and the most authoritative single statement; Taff 1992 pp. 137-143 is the explicit rule.

tone_statements.citation: Taff, Alice. 1999. Phonetics and phonology of Unangan (Eastern Aleut) intonation. PhD dissertation, University of Washington, Seattle.
tone_statements.quote: Language specific findings are: the isomorphy of words with intermediate phrases, a characteristic peak-trough contour for words, a characteristic 'cascade' contour for sentences, an apparent syntactic connection between noun phrase structure and intonation, and a sparse use, if any, of pitch accents since there is little evidence of pitch prominence associating with stressed syllables. Declarative and yes/no question contours contrast primarily in sentence-final voicing. A phonological account of the findings is provided using a two-level tone system. The tone inventory includes a H* pitch accent, H, L, LH, and ↑H phrase accents, and L% and H% boundary tones.
tone_statements.summary: Pitch analysed as intonation only (two-level model): H, L, LH phrase accents, L% H% boundary tones, sparse H* accents if any, as pitch prominence rarely sits on stressed syllables. Penultimate stress.

sources.note: Sec. 1.2.2.1 'Stress and quantity' pp. 30-31: stress not phonemic; largely determined by syllable weight (vowel length), consonant sonority and rhythm; disyllables stress the initial unless the 2nd vowel is long; Eastern tends to penult if final is short, Atkan tends to initial; initial syllable often carries more-than-weakest (delimiting) stress. Sec. 1.6.1 p. 45: emphatic initial stress; 1.6.2 exclamatory final lengthening.

sources.citation: Rozelle, Lorna. 1997. The effect of stress on vowel length in Aleut. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 95: 91-101.
sources.quote: Aleut has a quantity sensitive stress system. Taff (1992) states weight is assigned at the nuclear level so that consonants are weightless. Syllables containing long vowels are heavy, and syllables containing short vowels are light. Stress falls on the ultimate syllable if it is heavy and the penultimate syllable is light, (2a). Otherwise, stress falls on the penultimate syllable, (2b and 2c). [p.91] ... All vowels are short, and in each case, the vowel with greatest duration is the penultimate, not the antepenultimate, indicating that the penultimate syllable is stressed. Words receive stress before the final syllable is deleted. [p.97]
sources.locator: sec. 1.1 p. 91 (stress rule); sec. 3 pp. 95-96 (durations); sec. 4 p. 97 (final-syllable deletion); summary p. 99
sources.note: p. 91: 'Aleut has a quantity sensitive stress system.. Stress falls on the ultimate syllable if it is heavy and the penultimate syllable is light. Otherwise, stress falls on the penultimate syllable'; duration is a correlate of stress; length contrast maintained; stress assigned before final-syllable deletion (Pribilof speakers).

sources.quote: The Aleut (abbreviated as A) prosodic pattern has been considered rather simple when compared with its cognate Eskimo languages, because the primary stress (´) accent falls on the penultimate mora and the secondary stress (`) accent falls on the initial mora, with lengthening and gemination not being distinctive. [p.149] ... At the Conference in 1990 Knut Bergsland stated that stress is fluctuating and largely determined by vowel length and consonantic sonority and in EA it is frequently, but far from generally penultimate, while in Atka and Attu dialects it is more often initial. [p.149 fn.3]
sources.locator: sec. 0 Introduction p. 149 and footnotes 2-3; sec. 1.1 p. 151; sec. 2.2 p. 154 (cyclic even-mora stress)
sources.note: Umnak (Eastern) Aleut, p. 150: 'Aleut has two prominent stress accents.. secondary stress falls on the first mora marking the beginning of the word and the primary stress, accompanied by the peak of pitch, falls on the penultimate mora'; reports Bergsland (1990 conference) as saying stress is fluctuating, frequently but far from generally penultimate in Eastern and more often initial in Atka/Attu.

sources.citation: Golovko, E. V. 1997. Aleutskij jazyk. In A. P. Volodin et al. (eds.), Jazyki mira: Paleoaziatskie jazyki, 101-116. Moscow: Indrik. (excerpt pp. 104-105, sec. 2.1.2)
sources.note: p. 104, sec. 2.1.2 (Russian): length is not a correlate of word or phrase stress; rhythmic structure = regular alternation of accented and neutral syllables; CVCVC forms without long vowels accent the first syllable, trisyllables the middle syllable in isolation, four-syllable forms the 1st and 3rd; a long vowel resets the count; distribution varies with syntactic context; accented syllables lengthen the following sonorant.

sources.citation: Bergsland, Knut. 1983. Preliminary notes on Aleut prosody. Typescript dated December 9, 1983, 2 pp. Alaska Native Language Center.
sources.quote: Atkan (and Attuan). The stress is fluctuating, e.g. both 'ataqan and a'taqan, depending (presumably) on the rythm of the context. Usually, however, the initial syllable will have "some" stress, but the stress also depends upon the relative sonority of the syllables, that is, vowel length, e.g. ,a'daa (or 'a,daa) 'his/her father' vs. 'adang 'my father'; or consonantic sonority ... Eastern. In general, one could say, the penultimate "mora" (short vowel = 1 mora, long vowel = 2 more) has at least "some" stress, e.g. 'adang, a'daa, more or less as in Atkan. In tri- and quadrisyllabic forms, however, also the antepenult (mora) may have the main stress, and there is fluctuation
sources.note: Atkan/Attuan: stress fluctuating (both 'ataqan and a'taqan), usually some stress on the initial, attracted by vowel length and consonant sonority. Eastern: 'the penultimate mora (short vowel = 1 mora, long vowel = 2) has at least some stress', antepenult may take main stress in 3-4 syllable forms; syncopation rules.

sources.citation: Bergsland, Knut (comp.). 1994. Aleut Dictionary / Unangam Tunudgusii. An Unabridged Lexicon of the Aleutian, Pribilof, and Commander Islands Aleut Language. Fairbanks: ANLC. Introduction sec. 2.5 'Stress and related features of pronunciation', p. xx.
sources.note: 'Stress in Aleut is somewhat indeterminate and difficult to define'; 'In Eastern Aleut the stronger stress tends to fall on the next to the last syllable of a word if the last one is short (has a short vowel), on the last syllable if it is long (has a long vowel), and a weaker stress frequently falls on the first syllable'; in Atkan and Attuan stronger stress on the first syllable is more prevalent; long vowels, sonorous consonants, closed syllables and rhythm can shift it; expressive final stress in exclamations.

sources.citation: Taff, Alice. 1992. Primary Stress in Aleut. University of Washington Working Papers in Linguistics 10 (supplement: Papers from NWLC VIII), pp. 137-145.
sources.quote: Aleut is one of the languages in which primary stress is too regular to have generated much analytical interest. Investigators have simply noted the predominately penultimate primary stress as well as some relationship between long vowels and stress. [p.137] ... Final syllables are stressed when heavy as in 4) ... unless the penult is also heavy as in 5). [pp.138-139] ... The best solution for assigning stress to Aleut words in citation form is 18): a. Assign moraic trochees from R->L iteratively b. with HFE (triggered by two final neighboring strong stresses) c. and application of End Rule Right. [p.143]
sources.locator: p. 137 (intro), p. 139 exx. 5-7, p. 143 rule (18); pp. 3, 4, 9. p. 138 is partly covered by an archive card in the scan.
sources.note: Pribilof (Eastern) Aleut: quantity-sensitive; long vowels heavy, consonants weightless; primary stress 'hovers around the right two syllables' (penult, or a heavy ultima), analysed with right-to-left moraic feet and End Rule Right; rhythmic secondary stresses show iteration; final-rime truncation keeps penultimate stress. Quotes Geoghegan 1944:10 ('generally falls on the penult') and Bergsland 1956:39, 1990:36.

sources.citation: Oshima, Minoru. 1990. Prosody and Syncopation in Eastern Aleut. Papers from the Seventh Inuit Studies Conference, Fairbanks, 19-23 August 1990 (Inuit Studies Occasional Papers 4), 303-311.
sources.quote: The Aleut prosodic pattern of words has been considered rather simple, because the primary stress accent falls on the penultimate syllable or mora and the secondary stress accent falls on the initial syllable or mora, and lengthening and gemination are not distinctive unlike what is the case in Eskimo languages. [p.303] ... The stress accent cyclically falls on the even-numbered syllable backwards from the primarily stressed syllable in CV strings. As a result the odd-numbered syllable is unstressed and optionally (in a rapid speech style) syncopated. [p.305]
sources.locator: sec. 0 Introduction p. 303; sec. 3-2 Syncopation Rule 2 p. 305; sec. 5 Conclusion and fn. 1 p. 310
sources.note: p. 303: 'the primary stress accent falls on the penultimate syllable or mora and the secondary stress accent falls on the initial syllable or mora'; secondary stresses on alternate syllables backwards from the primary; syncopation of unstressed vowels.

sources.citation: Asinovsky, A. S. & E. V. Golovko. 1987. Rhythmic Accent Patterns in Aleut. Proceedings of the XIth International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Tallinn, 1-7 August 1987, Se 8.5.1-8.5.3 (pp. 174-176).
sources.quote: Aleut, being a language without a word-stress, forms its rhythmic structure by means of two main things: rhythmic accent and long vowels. There are several main rhythmic accent patterns in Aleut, long vowels "breaking ranks" - then, rhythmic accent is counted from that "break". [p.174] ... In wordforms of CVCVC-structure (if they do not include long vowels), the first syllable is constantly accented ... In multi-syllable wordforms a rule of rhythmic accent puts an accent on every second syllable, except in the cases when a long vowel appears and breaks the rhythmic structure; then, rhythmic accent is counted from that "rhythmic break". [p.175]
sources.locator: Abstract and Introduction, Se 8.5.1 (p. 174); 'Accent and rhythmic structure', Se 8.5.2 (p. 175); conclusion Se 8.5.3 (p. 176)
sources.note: Bering Island (Commander Islands) Aleut = conservative Atkan dialect, fieldwork 1982 and 1985. Claims Aleut has no word stress: prominence is a rhythmic alternating accent (every second syllable, counted anew from each long vowel), CVCVC words accented on the first syllable, three-syllable words tend to accent the second; accent is governed by the syntactic stretch ('there are no prosodic means in Aleut which provide conditions for the wordform as an independent unit', p.176). Contradicts the penultimate-stress reading of Eastern Aleut but agrees with Bergsland on fluctuation and long-vowel a…

sources.citation: Asinovsky, A. S. & E. V. Golovko. 1987. Rhythmic accent patterns in Aleut. Proceedings of the XIth International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Tallinn, vol. 5, Se 8.5.1-8.5.3 (pp. 174-176).
sources.note: Bering Island (Commander) Aleut: 'Aleut, being a language without a word-stress, forms its rhythmic structure by means of two main things: rhythmic accent and long vowels'; accent alternates on every other syllable counted from a long vowel ('break'); accented syllables lengthen the following sonorant.

sources.citation: Henry, Victor. 1879. Esquisse d'une grammaire raisonnee de la langue aleoute d'apres la grammaire et le vocabulaire de Ivan Veniaminov. Paris: Maisonneuve.
sources.note: Accent marks encode vowel length (pp. 4-5); p. 44 notes that in the apocopated (relative/possessed) noun form 'l'accent tonique se transporte ordinairement sur la derniere voyelle du theme, qui s'allonge' (adakh > ada). No general word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Veniaminov, Ioann. 1846. Opyt grammatiki aleutsko-lis'evskago jazyka. St Petersburg: Imperial Academy of Sciences.
sources.note: Section 'O slogoudarenii' (p. 82) states there is no need to give rules of syllable stress because long and short syllables are marked with diacritics throughout; the diacritic section (par. 5-7) treats the marks as length/stress signs. No placement rule.

sources.citation: Taff, Alice & Jacob Wegelin. 1998. Intonation of noun phrases in Unangan (Eastern Aleut). Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 103(5, Supplement): 2889 (135th ASA meeting abstract).
sources.note: Pitch tracks of ~20 sentences x 12 speakers, smoothed statistically; each Unangan word reaches a pitch maximum in its first half and ends lower than it starts, sentences down-trend into a 'cascade' of word steps; in possessor/possessed NPs the second word is higher in pitch than the first, contrary to the general lowering, so intonation is closely tied to syntax. Intonational pitch only; no lexical tone at issue. Abstract-only work, no quote taken.

sources.citation: Taff, Alice. 1997. Intonation patterns in Unangan (Eastern Aleut). In Intonation: Theory, Models and Applications. Proceedings of an ESCA Tutorial and Research Workshop, Athens, Greece, 18-20 September 1997, pp. 301-304. ISCA Archive (INT-1997).
sources.note: Claims (1) each content word is a phonological phrase with contour HL, (2) words are grouped into Intonational Phrases with boundary tones H% or L% (Pierrehumbert-style H/L); the word-initial H and word-final L are shown NOT to align with main word stress, hence analysed as phrase-accent/boundary tones of the phonological phrase, not H*/L* pitch accents; stress is penultimate or final and cued mainly by duration; also notes declination, range reset, final lowering. Pitch is thus phrasal, not lexical.

tone.quote: Main word stress is usually on the penultimate but can also be on the ultimate syllable [1], [11]. Stress is primarily marked by duration despite the fact that vowel length is contrastive in Unangan [10]. ... The central finding here is that intonation marks each word-sized domain. Each word has a H near its beginning. ... Therefore the H's do not appear to be H* pitch accents associating with main word stress. ... Therefore, these H's and L's are analysed as phrase accent boundary tones associating with PP boundary edges, H's marking the phrase beginnings and L's marking the phrase endings.
tone.locator: sec. 1 'Introduction' p. 301 and sec. 4.1 'Word contours' p. 303 (proceedings pagination 301-304)
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: No lexical tone posited: every content word carries a post-lexical H (near its beginning) and L (near its end) analysed as phonological-phrase edge tones, independent of the stressed syllable; intonational phrases end in H% (unfinished proposition) or L% (completed); declination, range resetting and final lowering observed; word stress penult/final, marked by duration.

tone.quote: Language specific findings are: the isomorphy of words with intermediate phrases, a characteristic peak-trough contour for words, a characteristic 'cascade' contour for sentences, an apparent syntactic connection between noun phrase structure and intonation, and a sparse use, if any, of pitch accents since there is little evidence of pitch prominence associating with stressed syllables. Declarative and yes/no question contours contrast primarily in sentence-final voicing. A phonological account of the findings is provided using a two-level tone system. The tone inventory includes a H* pitch accent, H, L, LH, and ↑H phrase accents, and L% and H% boundary tones.
tone.summary: Pitch analysed as intonation only (two-level model): H, L, LH phrase accents, L% H% boundary tones, sparse H* accents if any, as pitch prominence rarely sits on stressed syllables. Penultimate stress.
